correctness.rationale: For every fixed regular m-gon, n/P-scaled distances to vertices converge via independent endpoint Poisson processes to the maximum of m exact obtuse-angle chord altitudes. The fixed-\(m\) expectation converges by an exponential no-near-sample bound and exponentially small complement. Uniform pointwise bounds compare each chord altitude with \(\sin(2\pi/m)\) times \(XY/(X+Y)\), up to a relative \(O(m^{-2})\) error; expectation errors are \(O((\log m)/m^3)\). Conditioning on X yields the exact tail \(2ze^{-2z}K_1(2z)\) of \(XY/(X+Y)\). A Laplace saddle at u=z gives \(\sqrt{\pi z}e^{-4z}\)(1+O(z^-1)); this implies the stated Gumbel normalization. Two-sided global tail bounds establish centered-maxima uniform integrability, so the Gumbel mean gamma yields the correct second-order constant. Direct standard-library geometric and numeric tests (2894) were run; they supplement, not replace, the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Prior primary literature establishes random-polytope approximation, fixed-polygon Hausdorff corner-limit distributions, and only an order-of-magnitude regular-polygon estimate. The new statement is the subsequent vertex-number limit with a square-root exponential-tail factor, a nontrivial one-half log-log term, an exact additive constant and Gumbel fluctuations. The 2025 smooth-body Gumbel theorem has different curvature assumptions and varies the sample count rather than the polygonal corner number. Searches did not locate an implication already proved at the sharp two-term level. Residual risk of historically equivalent asymptotics remains.
residual_risks: Published exact fixed-\(m\) integral identities encode the distribution in principle; the distinct large-\(m\) sharp asymptotic may have been derived in historical work not found by these searches.
Related material outside accessible primary full texts could state an equivalent large-vertex limit; absence from the inspected sources is not mathematical proof of priority.

value.rationale: The growth of approximation error as polygon complexity increases is an explicitly motivated geometric-probability question. Earlier literature bounds its regular-polygon constant only up to factors. Determining the exact pi/2 leading coefficient, the half-log-log correction, the universal additive constant and the Gumbel fluctuation law exposes the structural extreme-corner mechanism. This is an all-m asymptotic classification, not a routine geometric formula or arbitrary numerical slice.
